newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia seen politically unready for privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Serbia seen politically unready for privatisation.

text.p: Serbia may be backing away from the privatisation of its state-dominated economy, regarded by most economists as essential to its post-sanctions recovery, independent analysts said on Friday.
They saw signs that President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist Party government could shelve privatisation plans at least until after presidential and republican parliament elections later this year.

Economists said the government, which planned to start privatisations from July 1 after launching a draft law amid fanfare in March, feared the resulting unemployment could cause damaging pre-election social unrest.
Ministers have suddenly turned silent on the privatisation plans and economist Miodrag Zec said: "There was official euphoria about privatisation (in March), but not any more."

Zec, a privatisation expert, added: "There is no more public rhetoric about privatisation and the (privatisation) minister did not attend an economists' gathering in Nis this week devoted to privatisation issues. That means something serious is going on about privatisation."

Another economist who spoke on condition of anonymity, said: "Both the law and the privatisation minister Milan Beko are 'on ice' until the Socialist Party decides what to do. D-day is nearing, but I'm afraid they'll put all reforms off."
Analysts believed the Socialists were still considering their pre-election strategy, estimating whether reforms and privatisation could help or hinder their chance of victory.
"If privatisation looks too risky, the law will bite the dust," the source said.
Analysts attributed a sudden turnabout on reforms to a recent reshuffle in the Socialist Party leadership in which the party was seen rehabilitating some of its ousted hardliners.
Sources close to the party said it was the hardliners who insisted socially-owned capital, a legacy of the past, retain its part in the economy.
Reformers have insisted the ownership transformation law should introduce compulsory privatisation.
But according to Zec: "There is no political will to cross the Rubicon and to make privatisation compulsory."
Privatisation sceptics appear to have been alarmed by the pressure for reform from Beko and Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister in charge of reforms Danko Djunic.

Beko and Djunic have also announced for mid-May a law tackling the repayment of more than four billion dollars in frozen hard currency savings and another legal document on rehabilitation of the ailing banking system.
Neither can be implemented without substantial external financial support and a debt rescheduling deal with Yugoslavia's creditors, economists said.
And neither seemed to fit into alleged attempts of the ruling party to further centralise the cash-strapped banking system and gain more control over scarce funds, they added.
Western diplomats cautioned that Milosevic risked losing any western support if he gives up privatisation.
"If that happens, there will certainly be no money coming to Yugoslavia and the economy already faces complete collapse," one Western diplomat said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
